findings.title: Auth bypass when RAGIN_REQUIRE_AUTH=false and API_KEY empty
findings.description: server_v2.py:_request_authorized() returns True unconditionally when REQUIRE_AUTH is False and API_KEY is empty. No warning, no log, no guard.
findings.evidence: Line 94: `if not REQUIRE_AUTH and not API_KEY: return True` — unconditional pass when both are falsy
findings.action: Add WARNING log when REQUIRE_AUTH is False at startup; add WARNING when API_KEY is empty and REQUIRE_AUTH is False; document in .env.example; docker-compose.yml should explicitly set RAGIN_REQUIRE_AUTH
findings.test_coverage: test_missing_production_service_key_rejects_app_creation tests the placeholder case but NOT the REQUIRE_AUTH=false case

findings.title: Legacy unverified serving was reachable (now disabled)
findings.description: server.py once served hisoka deceive/lure WITHOUT the mandatory verifier. Now disabled — _handle_deception() raises RuntimeError, routes return 410.
findings.evidence: LEGACY_SERVING_DISABLED = True at line 51; _handle_deception raises at line 89; deceive/lure routes return 410
findings.action: None — confirmed fixed. test_legacy_generative_route_is_disabled (tests/security/test_task2_verified_serving.py:156) verifies the 410 behavior.

findings.description: create_app(mode="standalone") raises RuntimeError. Standalone mode bypassed the harness pipeline. Now explicitly disabled.
findings.evidence: Line 357: `raise RuntimeError("standalone mode is disabled; use the mandatory verified pipeline")`
findings.action: None — confirmed fixed. The --mode standalone argparse choice and _init_component() function are now dead code.

findings.title: Cowrie SSH is a public attack surface
findings.description: Cowrie exposes SSH to the internet. While LLM backend responses go through the verified pipeline, the SSH connection itself is public. Attackers can attempt credential stuffing, CVE exploitation against Cowrie, or DoS.
findings.evidence: docker-compose.yml cowrie service: ports: ${COWRIE_PORT:-2223}:2222; cowrie-data volume; restart: unless-stopped
findings.action: Cowrie is intentionally public as a honeypot. Mitigations: Cowrie's own auth logging, verified pipeline for responses, network isolation for backend services. No code change needed — this is a deployment/operational concern.
findings.test_coverage: N/A — operational concern, not a code defect

findings.title: Provider credentials in environment variables
findings.description: Provider API keys (RAGIN_PROVIDER_API_KEY, RAGIN_HISOKA_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, AZURE_OPENAI_KEY) are read from environment. If the container or process environment is compromised, all LLM backend credentials are exposed.
findings.evidence: _PROVIDER_AUTH_ENV_ORDER lists 6 env vars; provider_api_key() returns the first non-placeholder value; server_v2 _init_pipeline reads api_key from env with fallback chain
findings.action: Placeholder detection prevents accidental use of template values. For production: use a secrets manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager), rotate keys, limit env var exposure in logs/core dumps. No code change needed for the current design — env vars are standard for containerized apps.

findings.title: Prompt injection from attacker input to LLM
findings.description: Attacker input flows into the LLM system prompt. _sanitize_input() strips 14 known injection patterns but only the FIRST occurrence of each. Sophisticated multi-turn injection, indirect injection via file content, or novel phrasings can bypass.
findings.evidence: _INJECTION_PATTERNS is a list of 14 string patterns; _sanitize_input strips the first occurrence of each; _DANGER_SIGNAL_PATTERNS has 100+ regex patterns; the verifier has identity-pin and fiction-contradiction checks as defense-in-depth
findings.action: Layered defense: (1) _sanitize_input strips 14 patterns, (2) _DANGER_SIGNAL_PATTERNS catches LLM output that reveals injection success, (3) FictionConsistencyVerifier identity-pin and fiction-contradiction checks catch drift even if injection succeeds, (4) deterministic fast-paths bypass LLM for most sensitive commands. Not exhaustive — novel injection phrasings may bypass. Acceptable for honeypot use where the goal is deception, not prevention of all injection.
findings.test_coverage: test_hisoka has extensive danger signal tests; test_verifier has identity-pin and fiction-contradiction tests

findings.title: mTLS optional and config-gated
findings.description: mTLS is OPTIONAL (RAGIN_MTLS_REQUIRED defaults to '0'). When enabled, it gates all non-public paths. But the default Docker Compose does NOT set RAGIN_MTLS_REQUIRED. The AWS EDGE↔CORE mTLS was a deployment-specific configuration.
findings.evidence: _validate_security_config checks mTLS; mtls_middleware checks RAGIN_MTLS_REQUIRED env; build_server_context_from_env requires RAGIN_MTLS_CERT_FILE/KEY_FILE/CA_FILE when enabled; docker-compose.yml does NOT set these
findings.action: mTLS available and tested (tests/security/test_mtls_transport.py exists). For internet-facing deploys, rely on NGINX TLS termination + API key auth. For internal service-to-service, consider mTLS in production compose. No code change needed.
findings.test_coverage: test_mtls_transport.py tests mTLS logic (not executed this audit)

findings.title: Session fixation via transcript-prefix session resolution
findings.description: The Cowrie bridge resolves sessions by content-prefix matching in an in-memory dict (_TRANSCRIPT_MAP, max 20K entries). An attacker who knows a previous session's transcript could craft a message list matching a prefix and hijack that session's context.
findings.evidence: _TRANSCRIPT_MAP is a dict mapping message tuples to session IDs; _resolve_bridge_session searches for the longest prefix match; _remember_bridge_session stores new mappings; max 20K entries; full clear when full
findings.action: X-Session-Id header (set by previous responses) wins over transcript-prefix resolution. Session_token (X-Session-Token) required for session-command API access. For field deploys: P1-2 remediation (fix _TRANSCRIPT_MAP for long-running deploys). The transcript-prefix fallback is necessary for Cowrie's LLM backend which doesn't send session headers.
findings.test_coverage: test_cowrie_bridge_transcript_prefix_resumes_session and test_cowrie_bridge_divergent_transcript_gets_fresh_session verify the prefix resolution behavior

findings.title: Rate limiting only in server.py, not server_v2
findings.description: server.py has rate_limit_middleware (60 req/min general, 12 req/min lure). server_v2 has NO rate limiting middleware. A deployed server_v2 pipeline is vulnerable to request flooding.
findings.evidence: server.py has _rate_limiter and _lure_rate_limiter with RateLimiter; server_v2 middlewares list is [mtls_middleware, auth_middleware, timing_middleware] — no rate limiter
findings.action: Add rate_limit_middleware to server_v2 (similar to server.py). Add to middleware list in create_app. Exempt health/ready. Add test for rate limiting.
findings.test_coverage: No tests for rate limiting in server_v2

findings.title: host_fiction.json stores fiction state in plaintext JSON
findings.description: HostFictionStore persists to data/host_fiction.json (34KB, untracked). Contains session IDs, verification state, host facts. While data is fabricated/decoy, an attacker with filesystem access can read the full fiction state.
findings.evidence: save() writes JSON with atomic replace; data/host_fiction.json exists (34461 bytes, modified 2026-10-10 23:03)
findings.action: Data is decoy/fabricated by design — no real credentials in fiction store. File is in repo's data/ directory. For production: consider file permissions, encryption at rest if on shared filesystem. No code change needed for current use case.

findings.title: No CSRF protection on session endpoints
findings.description: Session endpoints use API key auth but no CSRF tokens. If an attacker can make a victim's browser POST to server_v2 API (same-origin or via CORS), they could create sessions or issue commands.
findings.location: ragin/server_v2.py: session_create, session_command, session_wake, session_replay, session_context endpoints
findings.evidence: All session endpoints check X-API-Key or Authorization: Bearer, plus X-Session-Token for session-scoped routes. No CSRF token. No CORS configuration.
findings.action: server_v2 is not designed for browser access — it's a backend API for Cowrie and programmatic callers. CORS not configured. API key must be known to caller. Low risk for intended use case. If browser access is ever added, add CSRF tokens.

findings.title: Unsafe error details in legacy-compatible endpoints
findings.description: The legacy-compatible classify/analyze/deceive handlers in server_v2.py return str(e) on exception, which could leak internal details. However, these handlers are NOT registered in pipeline mode — they're dead code in the default serving path.
findings.evidence: classify handler returns web.json_response({"error": str(e)}, status=500) on exception; analyze and deceive similar; BUT these handlers are only registered in standalone mode which is disabled
findings.action: These handlers are dead code in pipeline mode (the default). They exist for backward compatibility with server.py but are unreachable. If standalone mode is ever re-enabled, these should return sanitized errors. For now: no action needed, but document that these are dead code.
findings.test_coverage: No tests for these handlers in pipeline mode (they're unreachable)

findings.title: _TRANSCRIPT_MAP unbounded memory growth (crude clear on full)
findings.description: The transcript map grows to 20K entries then clears entirely. Under long-running field deployments with many short sessions, this causes periodic memory spikes on clear. No persistence across restarts.
findings.action: See P1-2 remediation: bounded LRU eviction, configurable size, session continuity via disk-backed Session.wake().
findings.test_coverage: No tests for memory behavior under load

findings.title: Hardcoded default identities in source code
findings.description: The 5 persona identities (user, host, domain, ip, uid, gid, distro, kernel) are hardcoded in deception.py. An attacker who reads the source knows the exact fiction identities.
findings.evidence: _IDENTITIES dict defines 5 skill levels with hardcoded user=webapp, uid=1001, gid=1001, and different host/ip/domain per level
findings.action: Identities are fabricated decoy values by design. HostFictionStore allows per-host customization. The fiction is meant to be convincing to attackers, not secret from defenders. If identities need to be configurable per deployment, externalize to config. Low priority.
findings.test_coverage: test_hisoka has identity tests; test_host_fiction has host identity pin tests

findings.title: UUID session IDs use 64 bits (below 128-bit recommendation)
findings.description: Session IDs use uuid4.hex[:16] = 16 hex chars = 64 bits of entropy. While UUID4 is random, 64 bits is below the 128-bit recommendation for unguessable tokens.
findings.action: Session access also requires X-Session-Token (secrets.token_urlsafe(32) = 256 bits). Session ID alone is not sufficient for access. 64 bits is impractical to enumerate (2^64 attempts). If paranoid: increase to 24 hex chars (96 bits) or 32 (128 bits). Low priority.
findings.test_coverage: No specific test for session ID entropy

findings.title: No input size limit on attacker command
findings.description: The attacker's command is extracted from the last user message with no size limit. A maliciously large message could cause memory pressure.
findings.evidence: command = user_texts[-1].strip() — no length check; but RAGIN_MAX_REQUEST_BYTES env (default 1MB) limits request size in create_app
findings.action: RAGIN_MAX_REQUEST_BYTES limits request size (default 1MB). The command is a substring of the message content, so it's bounded by the request limit. Low risk. If needed: add explicit command length limit (suggested: 4096 chars).
findings.test_coverage: test_cowrie_bridge_rejects_invalid_json tests error handling for bad input

findings.title: Field export directory created without permission hardening
findings.description: _field_export_dir() creates directories with default permissions (umask-dependent). Session transcripts are appended to JSONL files.
findings.action: Data is fabricated decoy content. Field export is best-effort (exceptions silently caught). For production: set directory permissions explicitly if on shared filesystem. Low priority.
findings.test_coverage: _isolate_field_export fixture in test_server_v2.py tests field export isolation

findings.title: settings.yaml ${...} placeholders not expanded by yaml.safe_load
findings.description: settings.yaml has OPENROUTER_API_KEY: "${OPENROUTER_API_KEY}" and other ${...} values. But _load_config() in server_v2.py uses yaml.safe_load which does NOT expand these placeholders — they'd be read as literal strings.
findings.evidence: Line 8: `OPENROUTER_API_KEY: "${OPENROUTER_API_KEY}"` — looks like envsubst syntax; but yaml.safe_load doesn't expand ${...} — the string literal is read as-is
findings.action: This may be a latent bug or intentional (the settings.yaml is for the LLM gateway config which may use a different loader). Investigate: does the LLM gateway expand these placeholders? If not, the OPENROUTER_API_KEY setting in settings.yaml would be the literal string "${OPENROUTER_API_KEY}" which is a placeholder. Document the config hierarchy.

findings.title: server_v2 metrics endpoint is a placeholder
findings.description: The /metrics endpoint in server_v2 returns {"status": "metrics placeholder"}. server.py has a real Prometheus metrics endpoint using prometheus_client.
findings.action: server_v2 is not a Docker Compose service, so its metrics gap doesn't affect the deployed stack. server.py services have real Prometheus metrics. If server_v2 becomes a service: implement real metrics. Low priority.
findings.test_coverage: test_metrics asserts /metrics returns 200 (status code only, not content)
